Etude du traffic aérien francais entre 2: Study of French air traffic between 2018 and 2025
\n En 2020, la pandémie de COVID-19 a:
In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic hit the entire world. With the successive lockdowns, the aviation sector was deeply affected by this crisis.  
    Based on the data released by the government, we will attempt to assess the impact of COVID-19 on the French commercial aviation sector and how it has recovered.  
    We will then examine the structure of the French network.  
    It is important to note that the following analyses are performed with the default filter values. For visualizations that show a single year, the last selected year is used.
En 2018, les aéroports français ont accu:
In 2018, French airports welcomed 81.2 million passengers, an average of 6.76 million per month. This figure will serve as a reference to analyze the variations during and after the Covid period and to see if this crisis has had an impact on our way of travelling by air.
    We chose 2018 as the reference year because it is the last full year before anyone had heard of COVID.

\n - Jusqu'en février 2020, les chiff:
- Until February 2020, the figures remained in the reference range of 2018, between 4.7 and 8.4 million passengers. As we can see, the decline began in March. Traffic fell by 55% in one month, from 4.8 to 2.2 million passengers. The decline peaked in April, with a fall of 99.7% compared to 2018. For the first time, total traffic across the country stayed below one million passengers, with only 0.02 million passengers in the first month of the first lockdown.
    - The summer of 2020 saw a slight recovery in travel, but overall traffic remains well below 2018/2019 despite the end of the lockdown. This suggests that travellers were afraid to travel and use public transportation.
    - In October 2020, the second lockdown was announced, and a further decrease was observed, followed by a slight increase until the third lockdown.
    - It was in July 2021 that the curve showed a real improvement in figures. Thanks to the health pass and the end of all lockdowns, the number of passengers rose to 3.9 million in August. The following summer, the lifting of all Covid restrictions increased the number of passengers to 6.35 million. Nevertheless, we are still far from pre-pandemic levels. Only in 2023 did the number of passengers return to normal.
    - Although traffic slowed down from 2022, this was no longer due to COVID but to strikes and social unrest.
    - From the Paris Olympic Games onwards, traffic can be considered fully back to normal. However, it remains on average 8% below 2018 levels.

\n - Le graphique nous a:
- The graph showed that traffic was gradually returning to normal. However, it does not tell us whether traffic had returned to the same pattern as before the pandemic.
                - The basic annual pattern is as follows: there is a dip in January/February, after which traffic gradually increases until July/August. Traffic decreases slightly in September/October and then more strongly in December. This trend is observed in 2018/2019.
                - In 2020, the heatmap confirms that traffic stopped. In 2021, traffic resumed in summer but remained fairly stable towards the end of the year. There is no sign of the usual decline in demand at the end of the year.
                - In 2022, although summer was very busy, as in 2021, the distinct seasons have not yet returned  
                - Although the seasons were rather unclear in 2024, 2025 confirms a return to the 2018 pattern. A summer peak and a winter drop can be seen again.
                - While COVID had an impact on how we travel, it didn't affect the peak seasons. Travel habits remain the same as before the lockdowns.
                - This heatmap, however, teaches us something. The curve showed that once traffic had returned to normal, it remained slightly below pre-COVID levels. Here, it is clear that the decline is spread over the whole year rather than over one or two specific months.
                - So there is a year-round drop in passenger numbers that we need to explain.

Index sur retour du traffic pour chaque: Traffic recovery index by flight type
\n - Les deux visualisati:
- The following two visualisations aim to show the evolution of traffic, broken down by type of route: flights to and from metropolitan France (including Corsica), overseas territories (DOM-TOM), the European Union and destinations outside the European Union.
                - The first graph shows the evolution over the period 2018-2025 (as shown in the first curve), but broken down by type of route.
                - The second graph shows the percentage of pre-COVID passenger traffic recovered.
                - In 2018/2019, the breakdown was as follows: EU (55%) > Non-EU (24%) > Metropolitan France (16%) > Overseas Departments and Territories (5%).
                - Flights to overseas departments and territories do not follow the seasonal variations seen in the heatmap. These flights remain fairly stable throughout the year, unlike other types of routes.
                - Since the first lockdown, domestic flights have kept the sector afloat, especially flights within mainland France. International flights have collapsed completely.
                - The second graph shows that while domestic flights in metropolitan France experienced the smallest decline, flights to overseas departments and territories (DOM-TOM) bounced back the fastest, reaching 61% of their 2018 traffic as early as February 2021, while the rest of the sector did not exceed 16% of it. This is due to the fact that border controls remain strict for international flights and to the existence of alternative means of transport to travel within mainland France.
                - It is nevertheless interesting to note that after the end of border controls in March 2022, flights outside the EU increased dramatically, to the point of being the first to recover their pre-crisis levels, thus exceeding those of the overseas departments and territories.
                - To answer the question of what is responsible for the decrease in numbers compared to 2018, it is domestic flights that are at fault. In 2025, the highest volume of domestic flights was 56% of those in 2018. European flights are also down, at 96% of their 2018 traffic.
                - The decline in domestic flights is large enough to lead to an overall decrease in traffic, while for international routes and overseas departments and territories, the figures have never been higher, with an increase of 30% in the number of international flights.

The Marseille–Paris shuttle lost 473,000 passengers (33%) in 2025.  
                - If, using filters, only domestic flights are displayed, there are almost no gains and many losses. Only six routes show a gain, and they do not even cover the losses of the Paris-Marseille route.
                - The DOM-TOMs, on the other hand, do not appear on the graph. This confirms what can be seen on the curves, demand is stable.
                - When applying the non-EU flight filter, it is clear that international flights to Singapore and other destinations are gaining popularity

Cette analyse nous a montré que le Covid:
This analysis showed that Covid did not have a very long-term impact on the sector. The data indicate that only domestic flights experienced a decline in demand. The rest of the sector has recovered fairly quickly from this international crisis, or even benefited from it.  
            It is also important to note that Covid is probably not the only factor in this decline. The dataset does not provide information on the reasons for the increases or decreases. COVID led to the discovery of other ways to travel within the country, it has accelerated the process, but it is not the only one responsible for this decline. Factors such as environmental impact and others, although not included in the CSV file, should be taken into account to explain this decrease.

\n - Nous allons maintenant essayer d:
- We will now try to identify the routes that drive the French network.
    - It is clear that some routes clearly dominate the ranking. New York, Madrid, Lisbon, Nice and Montreal are at the top of the list.
    - Among these routes there are long-haul flights that meet the needs of both business and tourism travel. This is the case for New York and Montreal.
    - The same applies to flights to London although the distance is shorter
    - Domestic routes such as CDG–NCE are also mostly professional trips.
    - Short and medium-haul routes (Madrid, Lisbon) are frequent and driven by tourism, hence their good ranking.
    - In conclusion, it is clear that some routes represent a large part of the network, supported by many smaller connections.
    - The previous assertion that Paris is the hub of the network is confirmed. You have to go down to the 36th busiest route to find a flight that does not pass through Paris and this route carries less than a million passengers a year.

\n - La courbe monte très fortement a:
- The curve rises very strongly at the beginning, then flattens. Only 38 of the 289 routes (13% of the total) account for 50% of traffic.
    - A small minority of routes account for half of all passengers, while the vast majority of routes share the rest.
    - The French air transport network is therefore based on a small number of routes, which means that if one or more of them were to close, for various reasons, this could have a significant impact on the sector.

    </br></br></br>
\n - Il y a environ 130 passagers par:
- There are approximately 130 passengers per flight on short-haul routes and about 248 on long-haul routes. Long-haul flights carry about 1.9 times more passengers.
    - The lower quartile of long-haul flights (219) is above the upper limit of short-haul flights (approximately 190). Three out of four long-haul flights therefore carry more passengers than almost all short-haul flights.
    - The middle half of long-haul flights ranges from 219 to 307, compared with a spread of about 40 for short-haul flights. Long-haul flights are both larger and much more variable. Short-haul flights carry at most about 190 passengers, while long-haul flights carry up to 422.
    - Long-haul flights carry approximately twice as many passengers per flight as short-haul flights, with both categories barely overlapping. Distance is an important factor. People fly more for long distances than for short ones.
    </br></br></br>
\n Le réseau de transport aérien fran:
The French air transport network is a hub centered on Paris. A few routes concentrate most of the activity.  
    This dependency is quantifiable: 13% of routes account for 50% of traffic. This is due not only to the size of the aircraft, but also to changing attitudes linked to societal issues such as ecology. Long-haul flights carry approximately twice as many passengers per flight.  
    The fact that the network is mainly based on a small number of routes could have a significant negative impact on the sector if one or more of these routes were to be closed for various reasons. One example that comes to mind is the closure of many routes to the Middle East because of the war.

**Limitations**
    - The data is filtered by the sidebar, the above checks only concern the selected data.
    - Rows with the same airport of departure and destination were removed during cleaning.
    - Only routes with at least 10,000 equivalent passengers per month, at least 3 operators and no operator above 85% of the activity are published. Small routes are missing from this government-published dataset.
\n **Points clés** (filtres par défau:
**Key Points** (default filters, 2018 to 2025)
    - The COVID shock was severe but short. Traffic fell 99.7% in April 2020 compared to 2018, and returned to normal levels from 2023.
    - The recovery is uneven. Flights within mainland France peak at 56% of their 2018 level, while international and overseas flights exceed it.
    - The network is a hub centered on Paris airports and in particular on CDG. 13% of routes carry 50% of passengers, and long-haul flights carry approximately 1.9 times as many passengers per flight as short-haul flights.

    **Implications**
    - Dependence on a few routes and Paris makes the sector vulnerable to a new shock (health crisis, war, closure of airspace).
    - The declines observed on the recovery cannot be explained by COVID alone. The data gives no causes, so this is an interpretation.
